Regarding the title *Jīngshū lùnzǎnyào* (Essential Compendium of Commentaries and Treatises on the Sūtras), these nine characters comprise six layers of subject and object, ranging from the broad to the narrow.
First, the subject-object relationship of the commentary:
the five characters "Vajra" and so forth are the object (*suo*), while the four characters "commentary-treatise" (*shūlùn*) below them belong to the subject (*neng*).
2. The Expressor and the Expressed:
This means that the word "sūtra" belongs to the expressor, while the four characters "vajra" and so forth are the expressed.
3. The Distinction between Expressor and Expressed.
There are two [distinctions]:

first, the distinction between the general and the specific; that is, while the *Sūtra* (the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*) applies generally throughout the entire period of the Buddha’s temporal teachings, the *Prajñā[pāramitā]* is restricted solely to its own section.
Second, the distinction between the broad and the narrow; that is, while the *Prajñā[pāramitā]* still applies across eight sections, the *Vajracchedikā* belongs to only a single sūtra.
5. The analogy of the agent and the object:
the *vajra* is the agent, while *prajñā* belongs to the object.
6. The compendium of the agent and the object.
The character "compiled" (zǎn) refers to the subject, namely the author of the commentary;
the character "essential" (yào) refers to the object, namely the correct meaning.
If the two characters "preface and sequence" (bìngxù) were added, it would constitute yet another layer.
The two characters [“explanation” (*shu*) and “treatise” (*lun*)] are the agents of action, while all preceding terms are what they encompass.
Furthermore, these seven layers do not transcend the categories of teaching, practice, and principle.

Specifically, the five characters—“sūtra,” “commentary” (*shu*), “treatise” (*lun*), and “preface” (*xu*)—constitute the teaching; that is to say, they are that which expresses, explains, and introduces.
The "Path of Prajñā" refers to contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*).
The character "compiled" (*zǎn*) pertains to persons, referring to the author of the commentary.
The essential character "Vajra" pertains to principle (*tattva*).
The "diamond-like" (*vajropama*) true nature is itself the ultimate truth (*tattva*).
The characters constitute the correct terminology, while their meaning constitutes the underlying principle (*nyāya*).
Having understood that the subject and object of this single title are free from attachment, one must further understand the varying depths of the principles contained within the title.
The Vajra has three meanings: namely, firmness, sharpness, and clarity.
Prajñā also has three meanings: namely, the true mark (dharmatā), contemplative illumination, and words and letters.
The term *sūtra* has three meanings: namely, permanence (*nitya*), threading (*tantu*), and gathering (*saṃgraha*).
The term *śāstra* (commentary) also has three meanings: namely, being loose (*śithila*), resolving (*viniścaya*), and spreading (*vistara*).

The term *śāstra* (treatise/discourse) means deliberation (*vicāra*), and it likewise has three meanings: namely, deliberating on principles (*artha*), deliberating on wisdom (*jñāna*), and deliberating on practice (*caryā*).
The *Zuanyao* (Essential Compendium) also has three meanings: essential meaning, essential practice, and essential text.

Furthermore, as for the three meanings of "Vajra," because it cannot be destroyed by any phenomenon, can destroy all phenomena, and possesses both illumination and function, it may be used as a metaphor for the three kinds of *prajñā*.

"Solidity" is a metaphor for the true mark (dharmatā); because, although it has passed through many kalpas and circulated through the six realms of existence, it has never arisen or ceased, and has never been diminished or deficient, it is called "solid."
Therefore, the *Heart Sūtra* says:
"The mark of the emptiness of all these dharmas is that they are neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing," and so forth.

The "sharp" (*li*) is a metaphor for the *prajñā* of contemplative insight (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*); it is called "sharp" because when this [wisdom] manifests, it illuminates the emptiness of all phenomena.
Thus, the *Heart Sūtra* says:

"When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty, and thereby transcended all suffering and distress," and so forth.
“Neither wisdom nor attainment” and so forth.
This clarifies the *prajñā* of words by means of metaphor, because words are able to explain and manifest it, thereby making the contemplation of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) appear.
Because it possesses these three meanings and thus resembles that vajra, the vajra is cited as a metaphor for prajñā.

Indeed, all Buddhas and sentient beings alike possess this prajñā; however, because it remains enshrouded within the bonds of affliction, its utility cannot be realized. If one can hear the teachings and achieve awakening through the power of internal and external cultivation, one will then be able to sever the afflictions and transcend birth and death. When the wisdom of principle and the fundamental nature merge in mutual resonance, one can give rise to great function, becoming no different from a Buddha.

It is like gold within ore that cannot yet be used as needed; however, once it is extracted from the ore, it can certainly be fashioned into vessels to cut through things. Thus we know that this wisdom is not absent in anyone, and thus we know that this wisdom is able to establish the Great Meaning.
What is now called *prajñā* is, in fact, the Sanskrit term for "great wisdom" (*mahāmatis*).
"Vajra" is the primary metaphor for *prajñā*; since both the dharma and its metaphor are manifested together, it is termed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
If one follows the title of the scripture, it should be fully rendered as *pāramitā*, which praises the merit of wisdom.
"Reaching the other shore" (*bān'àn dào*) is the literal meaning in the language of Tang (Chinese), yet this still reflects the style of the Western Regions;
if one conforms to the conventions of this land (China), it should be translated as "reaching the other shore."

The "other shore" (pāra) is precisely nirvāṇa; because it is the counterpart to this shore of birth and death (saṃsāra), nirvāṇa is designated as "the other. This intends to clarify that prajñā is the wisdom that reaches the other shore; such is the specific characteristic of wisdom.
However, this wisdom that reaches the other shore (*pāramitā*) briefly comprises two aspects: namely, the sudden (*tun*) and the gradual (*jian*). As for the sudden:

when this wisdom manifests, it illuminates the emptiness of all phenomena in a single kṣaṇa; this itself is reaching the other shore, and thus it is called the wisdom that reaches the other shore. Because it does not require the passage of many moments of time, it is termed "sudden."

Although those of gradual practice may suddenly illuminate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), they still habitually act according to their innate nature, allowing arbitrary conceptual attachments to persist. Therefore, they employ the wisdom of sudden awakening to discern and examine deluded emotions, diminishing them again and again until reaching the state of non-action (*wuwei*). This constitutes ultimately reaching the other shore; it is also called the "wisdom that reaches the other shore. Because it proceeds through many stages of time, it is termed "gradual."
Although gradual and sudden differ in their speed, both are designated as the wisdom that reaches the other shore.
Therefore, in its full form, it should be called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
I shall not elaborate on them here for brevity.
Next, regarding the explanation that the characters of the sūtra possess three meanings:
according to the interpretations of various schools, there are many such meanings, including "a gushing spring," "giving birth," "a carpenter’s line," and "stringing a garland."
If the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains only two meanings— namely, "pervading" (*gan*) and "encompassing" (*she*)—
it means to thread through the meanings that ought to be explained and to sustain and gather in those sentient beings who are to be converted.

Furthermore, more than two thousand years have passed since the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, yet his lingering influence still persists; that those who are able to hear the True Dharma are all [benefited] by this is precisely the meaning of the sutra’s thorough exposition.

Sentient beings wander aimlessly, not knowing where they are headed; that they may encounter the gateway of the Buddha’s teaching and all return to the correct course—this is precisely the meaning of being "sustained" by the sūtra.
Because it possesses these two meanings, it is called a sūtra.

Now, by adding the meaning of "permanence" to these two, they correspond to the three kinds of prajñā: namely, the permanence of the true mark (lakṣaṇa), the continuity of contemplative illumination (pratyavekṣaṇā), and the inclusion of written words (vyañjana).

However, this sutra was translated by Kumārajīva; its verses are pure and elegant, causing people to delight in hearing them. To this day, from the young and old to the high and low, they fill the world, and there are none who do not uphold this sutra.
The *Sū-lùn-zǎn-yào* (Essential Compendium of Commentaries) refers precisely to this single fascicle of commentarial text.
These commentaries include those by Qinglong, Dayun, Zisheng, Chenwai, and others.
A "commentary" (*shū*) is so called because it elucidates the underlying principles, discerns the characteristics of the meanings, and arranges the words and phrases.

As for the treatises—namely those by Vasubandhu and Asaṅga, as well as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, the *Guṇaprabha-śāstra*, and others—each of these treatises spontaneously discusses the principles of wisdom (*jñāna*), reality (*tattva*), and practice (*caryā*).
Question:
"Since there are already commentaries and treatises that explain the sutras, why is it necessary to compose this commentary anew? Answer:
"Because it compiles the essentials, this commentary was composed by compiling the essential meanings of other commentaries and treatises.
Now, the establishment of this 'Compilation of Essentials' (Zuanyao) generally involves two intentions: first, to accord with the sacred intent above; second, to harmonize with the human mind below."
This is intended to show that among various interpretations, there are those that do not accord with the Sage’s intent nor harmonize with the human mind.

"As for the first point: this sutra belongs to the school of Emptiness and Signlessness (śūnyatā-nimitta), yet some provide explanations by extensively enumerating the characteristics of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa) and the stages of practice (bhūmi-sthāna). This does not accord with the Sage’s intent, as it loses sight of the core tenet."
Therefore, the Preface states:
"Some incorporate [the teachings] into names and characteristics, clinging to phenomena and deviating from the fundamental tenet.
When some hear this school of emptiness, they immediately provide an interpretation based on a single flavor and the principle of signlessness; this, too, does not accord with the intent of the Sage.

Although the fundamental principle (zong) is without characteristics, its meanings are manifold; yet, if one explains it solely through a single flavor, this is to be lost in the branches while confused about the source.
Therefore, the Preface states:
"Some merely speak of the One Truth, looking toward the source while losing sight of the tributaries."

"In the former case, one deviates from the fundamental tenets but does not lose the lineage; in this case, one loses the lineage but does not deviate from the fundamental tenets. Each has its strengths and weaknesses, and neither is fully perfected.
Furthermore, there are those who indulge in biased views to provide commentaries; they fail in both tenets and lineage and are unworthy of evaluation."
Therefore, the preface states:
"As for the rest—those discourses from the breast and commentaries from the chest—they are not worth discussing.

Yet, although these various theories each have their errors and inaccuracies, because they do not provide a comprehensive and thorough exposition, they are all judged to be inconsistent with the intent of the Sage.

Now, in composing this commentary, I have not added further doctrinal characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa) so as to avoid deviating from the essential tenets; by explaining the text according to its own words, one will not lose sight of the lineage. Thus, free from the two aforementioned faults, it perfectly attains the middle way; this alone transcends all others and uniquely accords with the Sage’s intent.
However, as this present commentary employs exclusively the words of the Sage, the preface states:
"Therefore, what is here set forth does not attack heterodox views; this commentary is the milk of the treatise, not the curd within the city."

How much more so for the two Bodhisattvas, who were honored as the Teachers of the Successors (Upapadya), and the Successor Tathāgata, who was the Teacher of Śākyamuni Buddha? Thus, tracing back through successive generations, the Buddhas have transmitted this one to another, descending to Asaṅga and Vasubandhu without any differing accounts. Therefore, it should be known that this commentary is indeed the word of the Buddha; those who slander this commentary are the same as those who slander the Buddha.
Therefore, the preface states:

"Furthermore, since Vasubandhu and Asaṅga were Honored Ones who occupy the place immediately preceding [Buddhahood], why should later students harbor doubts, either adding to or discarding [the text]?

Next, regarding those points that accord with the human mind: the commentaries and sub-commentaries of various schools have not yet captured the underlying principle and are moreover overly verbose; this causes students to rarely dare to apply their minds to them, resulting in many who merely recite the words, but few who achieve a comprehensive understanding.
Therefore, the preface states:
"It has caused those who recite [the scriptures] verbally to be as numerous as cow-hair, while those whose minds have attained penetration to be as rare as a unicorn's horn.

Now, this commentary extracts the essential pivot points to directly elucidate the sūtra; when the sūtra and its commentary are combined, they fill fifty sheets of paper. It is suitable for both monastics and laypeople to devote their attention to it, and it can be studied by those of superior, middling, or inferior faculties. For these two reasons, I have composed it; this represents wisdom first followed by compassion, benefiting both oneself and others.
Thus it is titled *The Essential Compendium of the Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "with preface" (*bing xu*), "with" (*bing*) means together or inclusive.
"Preface" (*xu*) means to narrate; it refers to the narration and exposition of the meaning of the sūtra and its commentary.
Furthermore, "preface" (*xu*) means "thread" (*xu*), referring to a beginning or introduction.
This indicates that these few lines on this half-sheet of paper serve as the introductory thread for composing the sub-commentary (*shu*).
Second, regarding the author's honorable title: "Jing" refers to the capital, meaning great; it is the great center where officials, commoners, nobles, and the lowly all congregate.

However, "West Capital" does not refer to the northeast; it is because the Daxing Fusi Temple was located there that it was implicitly distinguished, and thus the direction "west" was not explicitly stated.

"Śramaṇa" is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "diligent and quiescent," which is a general title for the assembly of Śākyas, meaning that they diligently cultivate all practices and bring afflictions to rest.

The author clarifies that this is not a new composition; it accords with the words of the *Zuanyao* (Essential Compendium) cited above, for it merely narrates the intent of the former sages rather than being a separate work of composition.
For example, the Master [Confucius] said:
"I transmit but do not create; I trust in and love antiquity; I venture to compare myself to my elder brother Lao Peng.

II. Introduction to the Fundamental Tenets A. Introduction to the Praising of the Sutra’s Intent 1. General Clarification of the Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching a. Clarifying How Delusion of Reality Gives Rise to Falsehood i. True Emptiness (Zhēn Kōng)
Regarding the phrase "the mirror-like mind," to state it briefly:
the first line refers to the true nature being free from conditions, while the second line refers to conditions having no self-nature; this is roughly the meaning.
If one is to clarify this, one should first provide a brief correlation and subsequently offer a detailed explanation.
Regarding the brief correlation:

within these two phrases, the "mirror image" is the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*), while "mind and form" are the phenomena (*dharma*). Fundamental purity and primordial emptiness apply to both the phenomena and the metaphor.
The mind is likened to a mirror and form is likened to a reflection; as a reflection is what appears in a mirror, so too is form what appears in the mind.
Although the mirror manifests reflections, those reflections are fundamentally empty, which demonstrates that the mirror is originally pure.
Although the mind manifests forms, those forms are fundamentally empty; this reveals that the mind is originally pure.
What is called "originally pure" is precisely "nature-purity," for it pervades both cause and effect, as well as ordinary beings and sages.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* says:
"It cannot be known by consciousness, nor is it the realm of the mind; its nature is fundamentally pure, and thus it is revealed to all sentient beings."
This is a brief correlation.
To explain it in detail:

a mirror refers to the mirrors used by people in the human world. Among them, there are those covered in dust and unfit for use; there are those that, though clean, remain inside their cases; and there are those that are pure and free of dust or grime, hung high upon a platform so that the myriad images are all reflected therein.
Now, taking the latter as an illustration:
regarding the mind (*citta*), the explanations provided by the two schools—the Nature School (*svabhāva-vāda*) and the Characteristic School (*lakṣaṇa-vāda*)—differ.

According to those of the Characteristic School, some define the mind as "that which accumulates and gives rise" (*saṃcita-utpādaka*), because it is the eighth consciousness alone that gathers all seeds and brings forth actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*).
Alternatively, "mind" may be defined as that which engages in cognitive apprehension (*ālambana*), since all eight consciousnesses are capable of apprehending their respective objects.
However, what has been described here refers only to conditioned phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, and is not the intended metaphor in this context.
As for those who speak according to the School of Nature (Xingzong), it refers to the Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamentally and originally pure mind of one's own nature.

That which is clarified here is precisely this mind, for it is the root of both delusion and awakening, the common basis for both ordinary beings and sages, and neither the mundane nor the supramundane exists apart from it.
Therefore, it is established as the essence of the Mahāyāna in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Thus, the treatise states:
"The Mahāyāna consists of two aspects: first, the phenomena (dharma), and second, the meaning (artha)."
"What is called 'Dharma' refers to the minds of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas. Based upon this mind, the meaning of Mahāyāna is revealed."
It is further stated that based on the single dharma of the One Mind, there are two gates:
first, the gate of the suchness of mind; second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of mind.
Each of these two gates comprehensively encompasses all dharmas.
What is the meaning of this?
Because these two gates are not separate from one another: since the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) is the universal characteristic, it encompasses all things;
and although the gate of arising and ceasing is a particular characteristic, because it is the arising and ceasing that is identical to True Suchness, it likewise encompasses all things.
Since these two gates both rely on the one mind as their source, one knows that the myriad dharmas do not transcend this mind.
Furthermore, the Avatamsaka Sūtra, being the perfectly consummate One Vehicle, likewise takes this mind as the substance of the one true dharma-realm.
Therefore, that commentary states:

"The four dharma-realms are unified as the One True Dharma-realm. This means it is tranquil and vast, profound and all-encompassing, universally including all phenomena; it is precisely the One Mind, whose essence transcends existence and non-existence, and whose characteristics are neither arising nor ceasing.
It continues, saying:
"The Buddhas realize this wondrous enlightenment and perfect clarity, manifesting the attainment of Bodhi to reveal it to sentient beings," and so forth.
Now, this single mind possesses both essence (xing) and appearance (xiang).

In terms of *lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics), there are distinctions such as ordinary person versus sage, delusion versus awakening, cause versus effect, and defilement versus purity; yet in terms of *dharmatā* (essential nature), it is a luminous clarity that is never obscured, a constant awareness that is ever-present.
Nevertheless, this nature and these characteristics are neither identical nor separate.
Because characteristics do not depart from nature, they are identical within difference;
because nature does not depart from characteristics, it is identical within difference.
Because nature is not identical to characteristics, there has never been any distinction.
Because characteristics are not identical to their nature, they have never failed to be distinct.
It is because nature and characteristics are of one flavor that both identity and difference coexist.
This is like water, waves, and moisture; through them, the identity and difference of nature and characteristics can be known.
However, this numinous mind is fundamentally not any thing, yet it is capable of being all things; it is for this reason that the name "mind" is established.
What is now called "pure" refers merely to the meaning of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*); it does not mean that purity is designated by way of excluding defilement.
This is because the single mind alone penetrates both the defiled and the pure. Heze said:

"The single word 'knowing' is the gateway to all wonders. All dharmas are established in dependence upon it; as it is the secret treasury of gain and loss, it is the profound pivot of ascent and descent.
To describe the śramaṇas as being truly "ultimate" is most fitting.
What is now being discerned is precisely this mind.
However, the two types mentioned previously in the context of the Characteristics School (Lakṣaṇavāda) are merely one gate within this mind: that of arising and ceasing.

Because one must discern the differences between the shallow and the profound, it is necessary to evaluate and distinguish them; yet, when harmonized and comprehensively integrated, nothing is truly left out.
The metaphor for "original purity" can be understood accordingly.
Within this dharma, there are two meanings:
First, because this mind has been fundamentally empty in nature from the very beginning;
second, because although it is currently entangled by afflictions, it remains undefiled.
This corresponds to the "Gate of True Suchness" (*tathatā-mukha*) in the *Awakening of Faith* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*).
Therefore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"O son of good family!
The nature of the minds of all sentient beings is fundamentally pure."
"Because the mind is fundamentally pure, the various fetters of affliction cannot defile or adhere to it.
Just as empty space cannot be stained, the nature of the mind and the nature of emptiness are equally non-dual," and so forth.
The image is the myriad phenomena manifested within the mirror; form (*rūpa*) is the various dharmas manifested by the fundamentally pure mind.

Yet, the manifested dharmas do not transcend form and mind. Now, the reason only "form" is mentioned and not "mind" is threefold: first, because the phrasing would have been too restrictive; second, because the reflection is subordinate to the original object; and third, because the former subsumes the latter.

The first two [points] can be understood; as for the latter "intention," all phenomena do not transcend the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The single character "form" (*rūpa*) runs through the beginning of these five; thus, when "form" is mentioned here, it refers to the first while subsuming the subsequent ones.
Therefore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, every enumeration of all phenomena invariably begins with the term "form" (*rūpa*).
As it says: "O Subhūti!..."
"Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure, form (*rūpa*) is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) is pure," and so forth.
Although this passage mentions form, its intent encompasses the mind as well. Since both form and mind are thus revealed, the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*) are fully accounted for.
The meaning of "originally empty" can be understood through analogy.
Within the Dharma, there are two senses:
first, that it is originally empty.
The Treatise says:
"All dharmas exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought; if one is free from mental conceptions, then there are no appearances of any objective realms."
Second, one directly perceives emptiness.

Thus, all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are empty from the very beginning; deluded people do not know this and falsely cling to them as being existent. Nevertheless, even while they cling to existence, these things have never failed to be empty.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"If all phenomena were not empty, there would be neither the Path nor its fruit.
It further states:
"Because emptiness exists, all phenomena are established.
This single phrase also serves to resolve doubts, for one might fear that upon hearing it said that the nature of the mind is inherently pure, [one would misunderstand].
Furthermore, the *Fojing lun* states:
"This mind encompasses worldly dharmas," etc., on which some claim that it must inherently possess defilement and so forth, as it would be inconsistent to speak of it as pure.
The subsequent line explains that the reflected forms are fundamentally empty.
The meaning is this: if form and so forth were real, they would defile the pure mind; since form and so forth are empty, by what means could they defile the mind?
It is like a mirror reflecting a foul image: the foul image is fundamentally empty, appearing to exist while actually being non-existent; how, then, can it cause defilement?
Therefore, it is said that the mirror-like mind is fundamentally pure and the reflected forms are originally empty.
The *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra* states: "Purity has two meanings: [the first is] the natural purity of the dharmadhātu, and the second is the purity resulting from the removal of adventitious defilements."
"First is purity by intrinsic nature, which is its universal characteristic.
Second is purity through the removal of defilements, which is its specific characteristic.
There are likewise two meanings in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*:
First is purity of intrinsic nature, which refers to liberation through natural purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-vimukti*).
Second is purity free from defilement, which refers to liberation through the exhaustion of hindrances (*āvaraṇa-kṣaya-vimukti*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* translated during the Wei dynasty states:
“There are two kinds of mind:
first, the associated mind, which refers to all afflictions, sensations, perceptions, mental formations, and so forth;
second, the dissociated mind, which refers to the ultimate truth—eternal, unchanging, and intrinsically pure.”
What is clarified here is precisely the mind of intrinsic purity and the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya); therefore, it is called "originally pure.
Furthermore, these two phrases mutually explain and establish one another.
The preceding phrase explains the subsequent phrase to establish the meaning of the emptiness of form;
the subsequent phrase explains the preceding phrase to establish the meaning of the purity of mind.
If form were not empty, the mind would not be pure; if the mind were not pure, form would not be empty.
Because the mind is pure, form is empty; because form is empty, the mind is pure.
Since the two dharmas of form and mind are not separate from one another, one should know that it is only through the purity of the mind that form can manifest.
Just as a mirror can only manifest images when it is clean, but cannot do so when it is defiled;
and just as an image cannot defile the mirror because it is empty, yet in reality it does defile it. Likewise, because form is empty, it cannot defile the mind; yet in reality, it does.
The preceding and following phrases clarify the correspondence between the dharma and its metaphor, mutually reinforcing one another; hence it is called "mutual explanation.
Regarding the section beginning with "dream-consciousness":
second, this clarifies that what is falsely existent is precisely the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind (*citta-utpāda-vināśa-mukha*) as set forth in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
This [explanation] also possesses both the dharma (the subject) and the simile.
Consciousness is likened to a dream, and the objects appearing within the dream are likened to the objective realm.

Just as a person, after falling asleep and dreaming, perceives objects where there are no objects, so too does the mind, through delusion, become consciousness and perceive an objective realm where no realm exists.

Nevertheless, although objects appear based on dreams, the objects within the dream are all empty; likewise, although objects arise from consciousness, both consciousness and its objects are equally illusory.
As for the dreamer, they are as usual, yet being shrouded by the veil of sleep, their mental consciousness becomes dim and obscured, and in a state of vagueness, they form a dream.
According to the *Qieyun*, "dream" (*meng*) denotes the state of mental agitation; it is also said that what one sees while sleeping is called a dream.
This means that when the conscious mind is clouded and agitated, one perceives extraordinary things, which is termed a "dream."

Consciousness is fundamentally pure; yet, within the single mind, there is a sudden lack of awareness. This lack of awareness is delusion, whereas the nature of the mind is true. The union of this truth and delusion is termed "consciousness," which is precisely the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:

"Based upon the Tathāgatagarbha, there arises the mind of birth-and-death; that which is called 'neither arising nor ceasing' is in conjunction with birth-and-death, being neither identical nor different, and is termed the Ālayavijñāna."
"Having no beginning" refers to the very commencement.
This clarifies that this consciousness has no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
Although true mind and deluded consciousness differ in their nature as being real or false, if one investigates their source, both are equally without a beginning.
However, there are two perspectives:
first, as stated in the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra* (or *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*):
"Both afflictions and bodhi are beginningless."

This means that since the time this true mind has existed, there has been this deluded consciousness; it does not mean that the true comes first and the deluded later, nor that the deluded comes first and the true later.
If one says that reality comes first and delusion follows, then it would follow that the Buddhas must further give rise to ignorance.
If one says that delusion comes first and reality follows, how could there be a delusion devoid of reality existing as something independent?
From this, we know that both are beginningless; thus, the analogy of the dream is not equivalent.
It is rather like gold and its ore.
If one were to say that the ore comes first and the gold comes later, then it would follow that the discarded ore must be smelted to obtain the gold.
If one were to say that gold exists first and the ore later, then a pure golden vessel ought to be able to re-emerge from the ore.
Since both of these things lack a beginning, this can be understood by analogy with all phenomena (*dharma*).
Question:
"As the Treatise states:

'Based upon the Tathāgatagarbha, there is the mind of arising and ceasing. Since it says that the false arises based on the true, the false comes after and the true comes before; how can you say that both are beginningless?"
Answer: “Not so.

What is called ‘relying’ clarifies that delusion has no self-substance and is established by relying on the Truth; it reveals the meaning of the fundamental and the derivative, not the meaning of before and after.”
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"Because the Tathāgatagarbha has no prior limit, the characteristic of ignorance likewise has no beginning.
If one were to say that there are sentient beings outside the triple world who first arise, this would be the teaching of non-Buddhist scriptures.
The second point means that the substance of delusion is entirely empty, leaving no trace whatsoever of its arising; therefore, it is said that delusion has no beginning.
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"When the awakened mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic. This is precisely that meaning.
If one considers this meaning, the analogy of the dream is precisely appropriate, because when a dream arises, it leaves no trace.
Since there are these two points of view, it is said that delusion has no beginning.

However, within these two analogies of the dream and the ore mentioned above, each takes only a small portion to collectively illustrate a single consciousness; it is only in this way that the principle of its beginninglessness is fully realized.
The dream illustrates the phenomenon that has no beginning, while the ore illustrates the time that has no beginning.
If one were to employ only the analogy of the ore, then the deluded consciousness would possess substantial reality.
If one were to take only the analogy of the dream, then the deluded consciousness would have a beginning.
Since we now take these analogies selectively based on their points of similarity, the principle is fully established.
"Objects" refers to the objects manifested within the dream;
"realms" refers to the realms of the self, dharmas, and so forth, which are transformed within consciousness.

Regarding their "establishment as existent": for instance, the realms of oneself and others seen in a dream are certainly non-existent once one has awakened and reflects upon them, yet while one is actually dreaming, they are definitely existent.
If this were not so, how could there be such things as praising joy and censuring anger, or loathing suffering and delighting in pleasure?
Therefore, we know they do exist.

It is as stated in the *Zhuangzi*: Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly; for the duration of the dream, it completely supplanted Zhuang Zhou. When he awoke and the dream had ended, where was the butterfly ever to be found again?
When he was Zhuang Zhou, he did not envy the butterfly; when he was the butterfly, he likewise did not envy Zhuang Zhou. Each existed in its own state, unaware of the other.
However, according to the intent of that text, this was intended to demonstrate the equality of life and death;
what I have cited here, by contrast, is meant to clarify the meaning of clinging to reality.

This means that based upon deluded consciousness, the appearances of a self, dharmas, and so forth arise through transformation; when one awakens and attains thorough penetration, one truly knows them to be empty, whereas when one is correctly deluded, one invariably clings to them as being existent.
If it were not so, how could there be such phenomena as greed, hatred, affection, aversion, grasping, and relinquishing?
Therefore, one knows that they do exist.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Based on the transformations of consciousness, one falsely perceives a self and dharmas, which are like illusions and dreams.
By the power of these illusions and dreams, the mind manifests as various appearances of external objects; conditioned by this, one clings to them as being real external objects."

"Furthermore, although one perceives various things within a dream, when their root is investigated, they are found to be solely the dreaming mind; for when the dreaming mind ceases, all dream-objects likewise cease.

It is the same with phenomena: though objects are infinite, when their root is traced, they are found to be solely the single consciousness-mind; when the consciousness-mind ceases, the objective realm follows in cessation."
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"All phenomena exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought.
If one is free from mental conceptualization, then there are no appearances of any objective realms."
Thus one knows that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only; how truly unfounded would it be to think otherwise!
Consequently, all contaminated and defiled phenomena within the mundane world of the three realms arise from deluded consciousness; therefore, this consciousness is termed the "deluded root."
"However, regarding the sequence in which all contaminated and defiled phenomena arise, there are generally two levels:
first, the beginningless root; second, the successive branches and offshoots."
The successive branches and their ramifications are explained in the subsequent section on "Pursuing Delusion," whereas the beginningless root is precisely what is addressed in this present section.
What is called the "root" refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
What is called "ignorance" (avidyā) refers to the absence of the clarity of wondrous enlightenment.
Speaking in terms of its general characteristic, it corresponds to this consciousness.
However, fundamental ignorance possesses two meanings: namely, delusion regarding the truth and the grasping of the false.
Those who are deluded regarding the Truth do not realize that the True Mind is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished;
its virtuous attributes and karmic functions exceed the sands of the Ganges in measure, yet they remain unaware of their daily use, as if mad or intoxicated.

If it were like a treasure trove within the house of a poor woman, or a bright pearl within the garment of a destitute son, though they exist, they are as if non-existent, and one undergoes needless suffering.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"To not understand the primary truth is called ignorance."

Regarding "clinging to the delusory": the delusory refers to the five aggregates, both form and mind, which are like illusions and transformations, fundamentally lacking any substantial reality. Sentient beings recognize these as their own body and mind; because they reckon the unreal to be real, it is called "clinging to the delusory."
Therefore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:

"One falsely identifies the four elements as the characteristics of one's own body, and the reflected images conditioned by the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind. It concludes:
"From this, there is the delusive existence of the cycle of birth and death; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*)."

However, these two meanings mutually establish one another; when one is raised, the other is necessarily included, for they never exist independently. If one clings to the false, one must be deluded regarding the true; if one is deluded regarding the true, one must cling to the false.
"For example, if someone is confused about the east, they will inevitably grasp for the west; these two are established in relation to one another—this can be seen by reflecting upon it.
[The commentary continues from] "From this... and below.
Second, it clarifies the flow and revolution of habitual delusion, which corresponds to the second section on the successive arising of deluded phenomena, namely the secondary branches.
"By these [means]" refers to the cause; "this" refers to the consciousness itself.

Because of this, one becomes deluded regarding the Truth and forms consciousness, whereby all worldly objects manifest. Taking these objects as conditions, one gives rise to afflictions, creates karma, and undergoes retribution without end.
Among these, the four characters "afflictions, karma, retribution, and response" constitute the three paths.
Furthermore, within the various teachings, these three dharmas are termed the "three obstructions" because they obstruct the Noble Path.
They are called the "three paths" because they lead the mind in a continuous succession toward karmic retribution.
They are called the "three defilements" because their nature is not pure.
Furthermore, these three obstacles depend upon one another: from afflictions, unwholesome karma arises; and by reason of the conditions of unwholesome karma, one obtains bitter fruits.
The initial mention of "delusions" (moha) refers to the afflictions (kleśa).
Their categories consist of the root and the derivative.
There are six roots, namely: greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong view.

There are twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), namely: anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), vexation (*pradāsa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), and so forth, up to distraction (*vikṣepa*) and lack of correct awareness (*asamprajanya*).

To state it briefly, they do not go beyond the three root afflictions: greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*); these three alone are capable of bringing about the world of the three realms.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Driven by greed, hatred, and delusion, one gives rise to body, speech, and mind, thereby committing immeasurable and boundless evil karmas.

These afflictions arise because the preceding ignorance is deluded regarding the principle of equality and falsely identifies with the five aggregates of body and mind; it is precisely this body and mind that constitute the root of all calamities and afflictions.
Thus Master Zhao said:

"Taking heaven and earth as the standard for high and low; taking the sun and moon as the standard for east and west; taking the body as the standard for self and other; and taking the mind as the standard for right and wrong."
Laozi also said: "I have a great affliction: it is because I have a body.
When I am without a body, what affliction could I have?"
Thus, one knows that this body is the root of all calamities and afflictions.
Having grasped it as existing, one consequently distinguishes between self and other; based upon this body and mind, various afflictions arise.
One gives rise to desire toward all agreeable objects and gives rise to hatred toward all disagreeable objects,
acting as a sovereign in order to protect oneself.
Within these two [afflictions], not knowing them to be false and allowing them to arise spontaneously is termed delusion (*moha*).
If one investigates the ultimate cause of these afflictions, they all arise from fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
Next, regarding "karma":
although karma is immeasurable, it is generally comprised of only three types:
namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable.

Due to the preceding intensity of greed and hatred, one incites the body and speech to commit various evil karmas—namely, the three physical, four verbal, and three mental actions, totaling the ten non-virtuous paths of action.

There are those who have some understanding of cause and effect and, desiring the glory and pleasure of future lives, turn evil into good by observing the five, eight, or ten precepts, such as the precept against killing; this constitutes wholesome karma.

Alternatively, one who, weary of the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances of the lower realms, and rejoicing in the purity, subtlety, and benefit of the higher realms, cultivates impure dhyāna-samādhi; this is called immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*).

Although these three types of karma differ in their relative superiority or inferiority, they are all produced by a deluded mind and are thus subsumed under the category of the outflowing (*sāsrava*).
Therefore, in the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, the three karmas are summarized as follows:
"Because they all constitute saṃsāra, they do not constitute the holy path.
From this, we know that the aforementioned three karmas are all produced based upon afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the term "retribution" (*vipāka*): "response" (*ying*) is itself "retribution. Since the seeds of karma already exist, stored within the *ālayavijñāna*, one must inevitably undergo retribution when the necessary causes and conditions converge.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Neither in the void, nor in the midst of the sea, nor by entering between mountain rocks—there is no place on earth where one can escape and avoid undergoing retribution."
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Calamities sent by Heaven may still be avoided, but calamities one brings upon oneself cannot be escaped.
From this, it follows that wherever there is karma, there must be retribution.
Nevertheless, although the essential nature and characteristics of all karmic actions are entirely non-existent when analyzed, at the time of receiving retribution, there is never any error:
evil causes yield bitter fruits and wholesome causes yield pleasant fruits, as infallible as shadows and echoes.
However, when discussing the retributions of the six realms of existence in general, they may be categorized into only three types:
namely, suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.
Due to the cause of prior evil karma, one experiences the retribution of suffering in the three miserable realms, namely:
These are the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals.
By virtue of preceding wholesome karma as the cause, one receives the pleasant retribution of humans and devas, namely:
the four continents and the six heavens of the desire realm.
With the aforementioned immovable karma as the cause, one experiences the specific retribution of the higher realms, namely the realm of form and the formless realm.

Within these three realms, the bodies that experience suffering and pleasure constitute the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of individual karma; the superior or inferior environmental worlds (*bhājana-loka*) in which they dwell constitute the supporting retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) of collective karma.
The primary retribution consists of birth, old age, sickness, and death; the secondary retribution consists of formation, subsistence, decay, and emptiness.

As the physical world empties only to form again, and sentient beings die only to be born once more, this continuity from beginningless time until now has been unceasing. That they remain deluded and cling to these things is truly pitiable!
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"The three realms offer no peace; they are like a burning house. This is because retribution arises from the cause of karma; karma is produced by delusion; delusion is caused by ignorance (*avidyā*); and ignorance is the beginningless, single moment of false existence.

Thus we know that as for the sentient and insentient beings of the three realms and six paths, when one investigates their origin, they all exist because of the dream-like consciousness and its accumulated habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

"Accumulated" (*xi*) refers to inheritance, which carries the meaning of continuity; for through delusion one initiates karma, and through karma one invites suffering, proceeding in successive succession.
"Habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*) refers to perfuming (*bhāvanā*), which carries the sense of mutual emulation; it clarifies that afflictions and karma emulate and perfume one another moment by moment.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Because it is accompanied by the habitual tendencies of various karmas and the habitual tendencies of the two graspings, it is called 'habitual tendency.'"

Nevertheless, these two meanings necessarily support one another: that is, because they continue in succession, they mutually instruct; and because they mutually instruct, they continue in succession. Thus, it is said "to inherit and practice" (*xi-xi*).
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"When the preceding maturation has already ceased, another maturation is born again."

For example, suppose there is a person who inherits the Confucian tradition and studies its literature; it is precisely because they inherit the Confucian tradition that they are able to study the literature.
Furthermore, it is precisely because they study the literature that they are able to inherit the Confucian tradition.
Is not the principle of mutual dependence self-evident?
"Lun" (綸) refers to "lun-xu" (綸緒), meaning the warp-threads [of a web].
This signifies that although the karmic seeds of sentient beings are indeed boundless, they do not ultimately undergo the retributions of the six realms simultaneously.
Because retribution follows a sequential order, it is called "thread-like sequence" (*lunxu*).
There are two meanings to this:
first, it is like a person who has incurred a debt; the one with the greater claim pulls them forward first.
Second, it is like a person planting seeds; that which is moistened germinates first.
"Wheel" (cakra) refers to revolving: having been born, one dies again; having died, one is born again. Because birth and death do not cease, it is called revolving.
Or one may die in the heavens and be born among humans, or die among humans and be born as an animal, and so forth.
Thus, the *Anityatā-sūtra* says:
"Cycling within the three realms is like the wheel of a water-drawing bucket."
Moreover, these two meanings also support one another: by means of the threads there is the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*), and by means of the cycle of rebirth there are the threads.
It is like picking silk from a cocoon; because that thread-wheel turns without ceasing, it causes the strands of silk to emerge in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, because it is raised by a continuous thread that does not cease, the spool of silk is made to revolve without stopping.
Alternatively, the character "lun" (淪) may also be used, as its meaning is likewise applicable; it carries the sense of sinking or being submerged.
This means that because one has long been submerged and drowned within the great river of birth and death, it is called "sinking" (*lun*).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"If there are sentient beings who delight in all conditioned things and perform various karmic deeds, such persons lose their way regarding the true and eternal; this is called 'emerging for a moment only to sink back again.'"

In the commentary, the character "wheel" (lún) is employed provisionally as previously explained; regarding afflictions and karma, it speaks of their "successive accumulation," while regarding retribution, it speaks of its "revolving cycles.
Nevertheless, these pairs are mutually supportive: that is to say, because afflictions and karma are successively accumulated, retribution is made to revolve in cycles.
It is truly because of the revolving cycle of retribution that delusions and karma are habitually inherited.
Thus, one rides upon causes to evoke effects, and relies upon effects to create causes; cause and effect support one another so that they never cease.

This is precisely the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), wherein each preceding factor serves as the cause and each succeeding factor serves as the result.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* states:

"Due to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of various karmas, together with the habitual tendencies of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*), once the previous maturation (*vipāka*) has been exhausted, another maturation arises."
Someone asked:
"In this way, one gives rise to delusions and creates karma; does the length of time and kalpas for receiving retribution and transmigrating vary?
Therefore, it continues:
"It cannot be obstructed or cut off for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Dust" refers to the minute particles of dust from the ten directions when the worlds are pulverized.
"Sands" refers to the flour-like sand in the Gaṅgā River; it is said that this river is forty li in circumference and its sand is as fine as flour.

*Kalpa* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "time-period" (*shifen*). Although great kalpas and small kalpas differ in being long or short durations, they are collectively termed "time-periods.
*Mo zhi* means "to be unable to [do so]."
"To obstruct and cut off" means to cease and extinguish.

This refers to the fact that since sentient beings of the six realms have begun to give rise to delusions, create karma, and undergo the cycle of birth and death, even if one were to take a single grain of sand as a kalpa, the kalpas would not be exhausted when the sand is exhausted; and even if one were to take a single mote of dust as a kalpa, the kalpas would remain inexhaustible when the dust is exhausted. Since motes of dust and grains of sand are finite while kalpas are infinite, this continuity has persisted until now, unable to be stopped or extinguished; therefore, it is said that "none can obstruct or cut it off."
Although these two sections contain many words and phrases, if one considers the actual substance, they do not exceed five terms:
namely, mind, consciousness, afflictions, karma, and retribution.
The remainder consists entirely of statements that clarify the manifestation of truth and falsehood and establish the formation of saṃsāra.
The meaning is this: fundamentally there is but one mind; through non-awakening it becomes consciousness, giving rise to delusions and creating karma, such that birth and death are endless.
For this reason, the Tathāgata manifests his body and expounds the teachings.
Therefore, the Great Commentary refers to this as "the conditions for initiating the teaching.
In the sub-commentary (*shu*), from the words "Therefore, I...
onwards, the second section specifically clarifies the intent behind preaching the teaching, as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*:

"I observe with my Buddha-eye the sentient beings of the six realms, impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom, entering the perilous path of birth and death where suffering continues without interruption;
it is for the sake of these sentient beings that I give rise to great compassion," and so forth.
The explanation has two parts: first, the purpose of citing the Āgamas; second, the actual citation. Regarding the first: the initial two phrases indicate the manifestation of the Buddha’s body.
The word "hence" (gu) carries the meaning of "therefore" or "the reason why."
"I" refers precisely to the Buddha.

The term "fully pure" (*pūrṇa-viśuddha*) distinguishes [the Buddha] from those who are "partially pure," because the Buddha has eternally exhausted all ignorance and has reached the ultimate state of non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*).
"Awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to the one who awakens; that is to say, the Buddha is the person who has attained awakening.
If the Sanskrit term *bodhi* is translated as "awakening" (*jue*), this refers to the dharma;
if the Sanskrit term *buddha* is translated as "the awakened one" (*juézhě*), this refers to the person.
Since the present discussion concerns the person, it says "the awakened one."
Furthermore, "fulfillment" (*pūrṇa*) is the general term, while "pure awakening" (*viśuddha-bodhi*) is the specific term.

The character "one" (*-ka*) refers to the person; it clarifies that the Tathāgata is the one who possesses fulfillment and purity, and fulfillment and awakening. This distinguishes him from other sages whose awakening and purity are not yet complete. Only the Buddha, the Tathāgata, has exhausted all three obstructions and perfected the three types of awakening; therefore, the Tathāgata is titled the "One of Fulfillment, Purity, and Awakening."
If these two are compared with respect to sentient beings, the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, all Buddhas, and the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), there are two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
first, sentient beings are impure; the two vehicles and bodhisattvas are partially pure; all Buddhas are fully pure; and the fundamental nature is simply pure.
Second, sentient beings are unawakened; the followers of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas are partially awakened; the Buddhas are fully awakened; and the fundamental nature is simply awakening.
Now, within these two sets of four propositions, both cases correspond to the third.
The "manifestation of signs" refers to the marks of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). "Among humans" refers to the place where the manifestation occurs.

The reason for displaying these signs only among humans is that those in the heavens are so attached to pleasure that they have no means to arouse the aspiration for enlightenment; those in the three miserable realms (*apāya*) suffer such extreme pain that it is precisely a difficult situation for such an arousal; only among humans do suffering and pleasure coexist, and when confronted with suffering, one is certain to be able to arouse the aspiration. Therefore, when the Buddha appears in transformation, those in the heavens are like an illness that has not yet manifested—what need is there for acupuncture or moxibustion? Those in the three miserable realms are like a terminal illness of the vital organs (*gāohuáng*), which cannot be cured.
Among human beings, those afflicted by minor ailments can be cured with medicine; for this reason, the Buddha appears in the world.
Furthermore, there are four general types of manifestations of the Tathāgata, namely:
the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) for others, the Great Transformation Body, the Minor Transformation Body, and the Emanation Bodies that appear according to the species [of beings].
Now, to clarify who it is that expounds this teaching: it is the small transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Furthermore, there are eight manifestations (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*), namely:
first, descending from the Tuṣita Heaven.
2. Entry into the womb;
3. Abiding in the womb;
4. Emergence from the womb.
5. Leaving Home [Note]: at the age of nineteen. [Main Text] 6.
Attaining Enlightenment [Note]: at the age of twenty-five. [Main Text] 7.
Turning the Wheel of Dharma [Note]: after fifty-five years had passed.
[Main Text] 8. Entering Nirvana; [Commentary] at the age of eighty.

[Main Text] This treatise manifests his physical presence, clarifying only the signs of attaining enlightenment; next, it clarifies the preaching of the Dharma, which is the sign of turning the Wheel of the Dharma.

The appearance of the Buddha upon attaining enlightenment was such that his body was sixteen feet tall with a complexion like purple-polished gold; a halo encircled his neck and the *svastika* was emblazoned upon his chest. Possessing the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence, he was escorted by the eight classes of supernatural beings and revered by the fourfold assembly. Majestic and towering, his radiance outshone the sun and moon; his virtuous marks were so vast and manifold that they could not be fully described.
This minor transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is inferior and weak in appearance; compared to the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya), they differ as much as clouds and mud.
Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"The elder removed his precious, noble robes and put on tattered, soiled garments. The precious, noble robes are used as a metaphor for the enjoyment body, while the tattered, soiled garments illustrate the purple-golden body (*cāmīkaravarṇa*).
It is because sentient beings have heavy defilements and are unable to behold the supreme and wondrous body.
Since they cannot see it nor hear of it, it would provide no benefit whatsoever to them; therefore, out of great compassion for all beings, he manifests a minor transformation.
It is also as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"The impoverished son saw his father seated upon a lion throne, with a precious footstool supporting his feet; his wealth and nobility were extraordinary, and his majestic virtue was most supreme."
Seeing this, the impoverished son thought to himself, "This must be either the king or someone of equal rank; it is not a place where I can obtain wealth through hired labor.
The elder saw his son and silently took note of him.
...and so on, until it says:

"He immediately removed his necklaces, fine soft garments, and ornaments, and put on coarse, tattered, and soiled clothes; holding a dustpan in his right hand, he used this expedient means to draw near to the impoverished son."
This metaphor illustrates how the Tathāgata conceals his sublime body and manifests inferior forms.
The commentary first discusses the "lower" [teachings] below to clarify the establishment of the teachings.
Since these Buddha-activities rely upon this method and are mediated by sound, what benefit would there be if there were no verbal instruction and only the manifestation of signs?
The teaching first expounds the Small [Vehicle] and only thereafter the Great [Vehicle].
Someone says:
"This clarifies Prajñā; why then discuss the Hīnayāna?
Answer: "Although both are the Buddha's words, some are profound and some are shallow; if they were not contrasted and compared, how could one know their relative depths?"
However, the Buddhism of a single lifetime does not transcend the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; even the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) is subsumed within the Mahāyāna.

That which is taken as the fundamental principle by all these schools is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). Although they all share the same fundamental principle of dependent origination, there are differences in their depth and subtlety therein.
The Hīnayāna consists of the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, whereas the Mahāyāna consists of the causes and conditions of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Regarding these causes and conditions of the absence of intrinsic nature, as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty."
"Emptiness" (śūnyatā) is precisely the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
Now, because this explains the Hīnayāna, it speaks of the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing.

As for the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing: when the conditions for all phenomena assemble, they arise; when the conditions disperse, they cease. Since they both arise and cease, one can sufficiently know that they are impermanent (anitya).
Thus, it is not that the phenomena of arising and ceasing do not exist; rather, it is because of the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
However, when the Buddha appears in the world, he first teaches the Lesser Vehicle for two reasons of remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*).

Therefore, it is said that the counteractive to arising and ceasing is for the purpose of countering the attachments to a self held by ordinary people and non-Buddhists. "Self" carries the meaning of a sovereign master; since one speaks of arising and ceasing, it is known that there is no master. Where there is no master and no sovereign, there is no self.

The teaching of dependent origination serves as an antidote to the non-Buddhists' doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). As the non-Buddhists primarily cling to a substantial self (*ātman*), they also concurrently hold to spontaneity because they believe there is an agent who experiences [the results]. Since it is stated that things arise through dependent origination, they are neither a substantial self nor spontaneous.
To remedy these two [extremes], the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing were first explained.

This refers to what the Buddha taught during the twelve years following his initial attainment of enlightenment—beginning with the conversion of the five bhikṣus at the Deer Park, followed by the conversions of Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the three Kāśyapa brothers—which are found in the various *Āgama* sūtras.
Regarding the phrase "now awakened," etc.:
the Buddha’s intention in teaching this Dharma is to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Four Noble Truths.
This involves two kinds of cause and effect.
That is to say:
origination is the cause of the world, while suffering is the fruit of the world;
the path is the cause for transcending the world, while cessation is the fruit of transcending the world.
Suffering consists of the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering.
The three types of suffering are: the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā), the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā), and the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
The eight sufferings are:
birth, old age, sickness, death, not obtaining what one seeks, the burden of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), separation from the beloved, and association with the hated.

Accumulation refers to karma and afflictions, as explained in the section on "Pursuing Delusion. Cessation refers to the two types of *nirvāṇa*—with remainder and without remainder—which can be seen in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
The Path is the Eightfold Noble Path, namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
"Truth" (*satya*) means "reality" (*sacca*).

Just as the worldly truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*)—the phenomena of affliction and aggregation—are called "real" because they are without falsehood or error, it does not mean that being unarisen and unceasing constitutes reality.
It is taught that suffering is definitively suffering and the origin is definitively the origin, and for this reason, all four [truths] are indeed such.
Thus, the *Śālistambasūtra* (The Sutra on the Final Teaching) says:
"The sun might be made cold, and the moon might be made hot, but the Noble Truth of Suffering as spoken by the Buddha is real; suffering cannot be made into pleasure."
This is precisely as when the Buddha, at the Deer Park, turned the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths three times for the five bhikṣus.
As for the "three turnings": the first is the turning that demonstrates the characteristics.
"Indication" refers to manifesting the characteristics of ascetic practices and so forth, causing others to realize and understand them by saying, "This is suffering; this is the origin," and so on.
Second is "exhortation to practice.
"Exhortation" means admonishing and encouraging them to cultivate and abandon [defilements], saying, "This is suffering; you must know it; this is the origin; you must abandon it," and so on.
Third is the turning through realization (*sākṣātkriyā-parāvṛtti*).

Realization refers to leading others to have faith and acceptance by drawing forth what one has already accomplished, saying: "This is suffering; I have known it," or "This is the origin; I have abandoned it," and so forth.
He thinks to himself: "I have already known, already abandoned, already cultivated, and already realized; you should learn from me, and you too shall know, abandon, cultivate, and realize."

Having spoken thus, a certain class of individuals with inferior faculties were awakened by these words; they grew weary of the suffering of birth and death and joyfully sought nirvāṇa. They resolved their minds to practice diligently, employing the seven kinds of skillful means beginning with the five *sthānacitta* (stopping-minds). By severing the coarse afflictions of discrimination within the four truths of the three realms, they attained the realization of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Continuing their cultivation, they gradually severed the subtle afflictions of co-arising (*sahaja*) within the three realms, realizing the remaining three fruits and attaining the state of an Arhat. Thus, they caused the causes and effects of the mundane world to perish, while bringing forth the causes and realizations of the supramundane.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"For those who seek to become śrāvakas, he preaches the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths," whereby they transcend birth, old age, sickness, and death, reaching ultimate nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Commentary states:
"First, the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing are explained, so as to lead to the realization of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Since the Commentary has already excluded what follows [from this point].

2. Second, the summary judgment regarding the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*): To conceptually impute a governing master over the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as a whole is called the grasping at a self.
If one investigates each [aggregate] individually, and no essence of a self is found within the nature of form (*rūpa*) and the others, this is called the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*).
If one perceives the five aggregates as having a real intrinsic nature, this is called attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

If one realizes that the five aggregates are like illusions and transformations, lacking inherent nature due to their dependence on conditions, this is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*).

"Those who have already eliminated" means they have reached exhaustion; because followers of the Hīnayāna, upon hearing the teaching on the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, do not cling to a self, it is said that "they have already eliminated the clinging to a self.

"Those who have not yet attained" refers to those who have not yet heard the teaching on the causes and conditions of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and thus still reckon the aggregates (*skandha*) as real; hence it is said that "they have not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*)."

To speak fully, it should be stated that having already eliminated the grasping at a self, one has realized the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), yet has not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) nor eliminated the grasping at phenomena.

Now, because the text employs an elliptical abbreviation—whereby the upper [grasping] is negated and the lower [emptiness] is implied—one enters the elimination of the grasping at a self; this is precisely the realization of the emptiness of the self, while the non-realization of the emptiness of phenomena is precisely the non-elimination of the grasping at phenomena.
The sub-commentary (*śūtra*) intends to proceed below.

Second, the exposition of the intent of the *Prajñāpāramitā* has two parts. First, a general statement regarding the great treatise. First, the exposition of the teaching and the explanation of its intent: "The root of the illness" is a metaphor for the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Just as when a person has an illness they become uneasy, and just as a tree with roots is able to produce branches and leaves;

the meaning is that the two types of grasping are like illnesses, causing all sentient beings to lack peace and happiness. If one takes the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) as the illness, then the illness itself is the root; this is an *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (appositional compound).
If one takes the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) as the illness, then that [grasping] is the root of the illness; this is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent compound).

Now, however, the illness extends to both types of grasping, while the root is a metaphor for the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), because the two entities—the subject and the object—are distinct.

I am that which relies, and phenomena (dharma) are that upon which one relies; since the former arises from the latter, the former is not the faculty (*indriya*), for faculties are restricted solely to the latter.
Consequently, while ordinary beings possess attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*), they necessarily also possess attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*);
whereas those of the two vehicles possess attachment to phenomena, but do not necessarily possess attachment to a self.
Furthermore, while those of the two vehicles may lack the grasping at a self, they do not necessarily lack the grasping at phenomena;
whereas for a Bodhisattva, the absence of grasping at phenomena necessarily entails the absence of grasping at a self.
This is like how one can only perceive a person by first being deluded regarding a tree stump.

Prajñā is wisdom; in order to manifest this dharma, the words were left behind to form the teaching, and the teaching consists of written characters. Prajñā comprises the two types of prajñā: contemplative insight (pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā) and the prajñā of ultimate reality (dharmatā-prajñā).
Now, speaking in terms of the Buddha, both the Dharma and the teaching are collectively termed *prajñā*.
The intention here is this:
it is because the Tathāgata intends to exhaustively eliminate the root of sentient beings' disease of attachment that he speaks of the *prajñā* of the school of emptiness.
However, while the teachings of the Mahāyāna are immeasurable and boundless, why is it that only Prajñāpāramitā is discussed here?

It is because this is the primary gateway for correctly destroying attachment to the Mahāyāna; once these two attachments are eliminated, true nature manifests of itself. Therefore, only this [Prajñā] is discussed to eliminate their ailment.
Therefore, an ancient master said:

"The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is like the laws for governing a state and the medicine for nourishing one's nature; the teachings of Prajñā are like the generals who quell disorder and the medicine that cures disease."
Since these two sutras are thus, the others may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the "equality of mind and object":

the Buddha initially taught that in the Hīnayāna both mind and object exist; in teaching the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna, he taught that while the object is empty, the mind exists; in teaching the Prajñāpāramitā, he taught that both mind and object are empty. Now, this [text] precisely clarifies this point, and therefore speaks of their "simultaneous cessation."
The mind refers to the primary mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); the object refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) of the various consciousnesses.

The mind encompasses both the transformative (*pariṇāma*) and the cognitive (*ālambaka*) aspects; the object encompasses both the substantial essence (*mūla-vastu*) and the reflected image (*pratibimba*).
Because the distinctions between mind and object have equally vanished, they are said to be simultaneously extinguished.
This means that with respect to the imagined nature (*parikalpita*), there is absolutely nothing at all, like a snake upon a rope.
With respect to the dependent nature (*paratantra*), conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), like a rope upon hemp.
Because of the mind there is the object, and because of the object there is the mind; when the object ceases, the mind becomes empty, and when the mind is as it is, the object passes away.
However, although all dharmas are numerous, they do not transcend the mind and its objects (*citta-viṣaya*). Once the mind and its objects have dissolved, then everything dissolves.
The *Heart Sūtra* also says: "No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma; no sphere of the eye, up to and including no sphere of mental consciousness," and so forth; therefore, it is said that all are equally extinguished.
The phrase "it is precisely the true mind" clarifies that it is not subject to annihilation.
It is feared that upon hearing that all phenomena are subsumed into non-existence, one might conclude that since all phenomena are non-existent, they must therefore be annihilated.
Therefore, it is explicitly stated that this is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*).
However, this mind is not the same as the "mind" mentioned above; the former is the deluded mind born of conditions, which is the aforementioned dream-consciousness;
this is the eternally abiding true mind, which is the aforementioned mirror-mind.
In order to distinguish it from others, the term "true" is specifically used; for all phenomena depend upon this mind, and apart from this mind, no other phenomenon exists.
Thus, a sutra says:
"The causes and effects of all worlds, down to their subtlest atoms, take form through the mind."

That which manifests from the mind is called the dependent nature (*paratantra*); to grasp it as real is called the imagined nature (*parikalpita*). When both the basis and the imagination have subsided, this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).
It is like a rope that exists in dependence on hemp, and a snake that arises based on the rope; once the rope and the snake have vanished, only the hemp remains!
This is the Master of the Commentary’s elucidation of the profound intent (*abhiprāya*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
According to the scriptural text itself, it merely states that all phenomena are empty; it does not state that this emptiness is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*).
Therefore, the subsequent passage states:
"To be free from all marks is precisely what is called 'the Buddhas'. Although this meaning is not explicitly stated in the text, its reality is indeed such.
In the Faxing (Dharmatā) school, the true mind is directly revealed within the state of the emptiness of all phenomena.
Therefore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:
"All manner of illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment, just as flowers in the sky appear from within space," and continues until it says:
"When all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind remains unmoving. Thus, it is said that this is the true mind.
Regarding the phrase "both defilement and purity are simultaneously extinguished":
the preceding statement that the mind and its objects, as well as their defilement and purity, have already been relinquished was not yet explicitly clarified;

therefore, it is explained again here. The meaning is that not only are there no phenomena of the mind and its objects associated with outflows (*āsrava*), but even within those phenomena, neither defiled nor pure phenomena exist.
It is only to counteract defilement that the name of "pure phenomena" is manifested.
